# Craft floor

Load this after the direction is settled, and build without announcing the checklist. A pinned brief or the committed visual world overrides anything here; your own habit does not. When the design hook is active it already enforces the mechanical checks below as you edit: act on its findings instead of re-auditing each rule.

## Verify

Each of these is a check on the built result, not an intention. Run them together in the batched inspection rounds, not as separate screenshot trips; the checks share one render.

- **Contrast:** body and placeholder text ≥4.5:1, large text ≥3:1. On colored surfaces tint secondary text from that hue or the foreground; never gray.
- **Depth:** shadows carry an offset and a soft blur. A zero-offset colored halo is decoration.
- **Spacing:** tight groups, generous separation, more space above a heading than below it. Read the computed values.
- **Type:** body measure 65–75ch, display max 6rem, tracking floor -0.04em, balanced headings, obvious scale and weight steps. Run the real copy at every breakpoint and fix what overflows.
- **Motion:** one authored moment, not scattered effects and not one identical entrance on every section. Exponential ease-out from an already-visible default. Reach past transform and opacity: blur, backdrop-filter, clip-path, mask, and shadow belong to the palette when they stay smooth.
- **States:** hover, disabled, loading, error, empty. Plus real content, working controls, responsive composition, keyboard focus.
- **Copy:** the product's own language. Controls name their action; errors name the problem and the recovery.
- **Coverage:** every brief requirement present and findable within seconds.

## Refuse

These are the category's defaults, not bans: the brief's own words can earn any of them. Reaching for one when the axis is free means you were not deciding; recognizing that means rewriting the element, not softening it.

Page scaffolds:

- Same-size cards of icon plus heading plus text as the page structure. Cards are the lazy container; nested cards are always wrong.
- The hero-metric template: big number, small label, supporting stats, accent.
- A kicker or eyebrow above a heading. This one is a ban, not a default: no brief earns it back. The heading carries its own weight; delete the label and let the heading speak.
- Section numbers (01 / 02 / 03) unless the sequence itself carries information the reader needs.
- A modal for a task that needs neither interruption nor protected focus.

Surface habits:

- Gradient text. Emphasis comes from weight or size.
- Glass and blur as decoration rather than as a specific effect.
- A colored `border-left` or `border-right` above 1px on cards, list items, callouts, or alerts.
- Hard offset shadows (`box-shadow: 4px 4px 0`) outside a world that is actually neobrutalist. The zero-blur block shadow is a costume, not a depth system; a world that did not choose it never earns it as a default.
- Sparklines, progress rings, and soft-shadowed rounded rectangles standing in for content.
- Monospace as a costume for "technical" rather than for code, data, or measurement.
- A system display face (Impact, Arial Black, the platform sans) as the display voice of an own-world page. Source and self-host a face whose character matches the approved lettering; the closest installed font is a failure, not a fallback.
- Unicode glyphs or emoji standing in for an icon system. Icons are drawn, from a real library or authored SVG, in one consistent stroke and weight.
- Light or dark picked by category. Pick it from the use scene: who, where, under what ambient light.

The floor holds the mechanics; it never picks the direction. With every check green, spend the page on the committed world, and when torn between refined and committed, commit.

- **Alt text**: Missing or poor image descriptions
- **Form issues**: Inputs without labels, poor error messaging, missing required indicators

### 2. Performance

**Check for**:
- **Layout thrashing**: Reading/writing layout properties in loops
- **Expensive animations**: Casual layout-property animation, unbounded blur/filter/shadow effects, or effects that visibly drop frames
- **Missing optimization**: Images without lazy loading, unoptimized assets

- **Render performance**: Unnecessary re-renders, missing memoization

# Product

<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->

## Platform

web

## Stack

static HTML/CSS/JS, single self-contained file per edition, rendered to PDF via headless Chrome.
Delegated: chosen because the deliverable is a printed page, the data is a small pre-computed
JSON payload, and the file must survive being emailed and re-rendered without a build step.

## Users

Baylor Football, weekly during the season. Two editions of one report, same week, same data spine:

- **Coaches edition** — head coach, coordinators, and position coaches. Read in the Monday
  meeting room, on paper, in a short window, usually alongside film. They want what last
  Saturday actually says and what next Saturday demands.
- **Performance edition** — strength & conditioning and medical staff. Same week, same game,
  but the question is exposure and workload, not tendencies. Drives training-week planning
  and who gets watched.

Author and owner: Applied Performance. The unit has published football analytics to this
audience before (the 2024 `BU_Post_2024` EPA report), so the audience already accepts a
report from this group.

## Product Purpose

One weekly report, produced Monday, that tells Baylor what the last game cost and what the
next opponent will demand — in two editions cut for two audiences. Success is that it ships
every game week without hand-editing, and that a coach acts on something in it.

The predecessor failed on maintenance, not content: its source required hand-editing opponent
names, team colors, logos and the next-opponent block every single week. Zero weekly hand-edits
is a hard product requirement, not a nice-to-have.

## Positioning

Applied Performance is the only group at Baylor that holds both the football data (PFF grades
and snap counts, CFBD play-by-play) and the athlete data (Catapult GPS, VALD force plates,
Perch VBT). No neighboring group can truthfully produce both editions from one spine.

## Capabilities and evidence

Working, verified data sources — all real, none simulated:

- **PFF** — local DuckDB at `Football/PFF_Data_Project/data/pff.db`; 175,559 game grades,
  4.7M stat rows, 2023–2025. Carries per-player snap counts across all phases.
- **CFBD API** — games, PPA/EPA, advanced box (success rate, explosiveness, line yards,
  havoc, by-down splits), drives, plays, and in-game win probability.
- Not yet joined into this report, but owned by the same unit: Catapult GPS
  (`DataBase_GPS_Reporting`), VALD ForceDecks (`ForcePlate_DecisionSystem`), Perch VBT
  (`PlayerProfiles_FB_03-28-2026`). A GPS-to-snap-count join is explicitly deferred.

## Constraints

- **Print is the primary medium.** The report is printed and handed out. Every fact must be
  visible on the page; nothing may live only in a hover state. Fixed page sizes, page-break
  control, and ink-safe color are requirements. Screen interaction may exist, but only as a
  bonus on top of a page that is complete without it.
- **Zero weekly hand-edits.** Opponent, next opponent, colors, and logos resolve from data.
- Season window runs late August to mid-January; the report has no value outside a game week.
- Athlete-level data carries FERPA obligations (see `SpeedProfiling/AGENTS.md`); the
  performance edition names players and must be handled accordingly.
- Reviewer preference on file (Kenny Boyd): no blame-implying rationale and no judgmental
  tier labels. Workload bands and player flags must read as descriptive, never as a verdict
  on the athlete.

## Terminology

EPA / PPA (expected points added per play), success rate, explosiveness, line yards, havoc
rate, stuff rate, snap count, exposure, workload baseline. Power Four = SEC, Big Ten, Big 12,
ACC — the comparison set for all percentiles.

## Open decisions

- Whether the two editions ship as two documents or one document with a split section.
- Whether the GPS/force-plate/VBT join enters the performance edition this season or next.

# Product

<!-- impeccable:product-schema 1 -->

## Platform

web

## Stack

static HTML/CSS/JS, single self-contained file per edition, rendered to PDF via headless Chrome.
Delegated: chosen because the deliverable is a printed page, the data is a small pre-computed
JSON payload, and the file must survive being emailed and re-rendered without a build step.

## Users

Baylor Football, weekly during the season. Two editions of one report, same week, same data spine:

- **Coaches edition** — head coach, coordinators, and position coaches. Read in the Monday
  meeting room, on paper, in a short window, usually alongside film. They want what last
  Saturday actually says and what next Saturday demands.
- **Performance edition** — strength & conditioning and medical staff. Same week, same game,
  but the question is exposure and workload, not tendencies. Drives training-week planning
  and who gets watched.

Author and owner: Applied Performance. The unit has published football analytics to this
audience before (the 2024 `BU_Post_2024` EPA report), so the audience already accepts a
report from this group.

## Product Purpose

One weekly report, produced Monday, that tells Baylor what the last game cost and what the
next opponent will demand — in two editions cut for two audiences. Success is that it ships
every game week without hand-editing, and that a coach acts on something in it.

The predecessor failed on maintenance, not content: its source required hand-editing opponent
names, team colors, logos and the next-opponent block every single week. Zero weekly hand-edits
is a hard product requirement, not a nice-to-have.

## Positioning

Applied Performance is the only group at Baylor that holds both the football data (PFF grades
and snap counts, CFBD play-by-play) and the athlete data (Catapult GPS, VALD force plates,
Perch VBT). No neighboring group can truthfully produce both editions from one spine.

## Capabilities and evidence

Working, verified data sources — all real, none simulated:

- **PFF** — local DuckDB at `Football/PFF_Data_Project/data/pff.db`; 175,559 game grades,
  4.7M stat rows, 2023–2025. Carries per-player snap counts across all phases.
- **CFBD API** — games, PPA/EPA, advanced box (success rate, explosiveness, line yards,
  havoc, by-down splits), drives, plays, and in-game win probability.
- Not yet joined into this report, but owned by the same unit: Catapult GPS
  (`DataBase_GPS_Reporting`), VALD ForceDecks (`ForcePlate_DecisionSystem`), Perch VBT
  (`PlayerProfiles_FB_03-28-2026`). A GPS-to-snap-count join is explicitly deferred.

## Constraints

- **Print is the primary medium.** The report is printed and handed out. Every fact must be
  visible on the page; nothing may live only in a hover state. Fixed page sizes, page-break
  control, and ink-safe color are requirements. Screen interaction may exist, but only as a
  bonus on top of a page that is complete without it.
- **Zero weekly hand-edits.** Opponent, next opponent, colors, and logos resolve from data.
- Season window runs late August to mid-January; the report has no value outside a game week.
- Athlete-level data carries FERPA obligations (see `SpeedProfiling/AGENTS.md`); the
  performance edition names players and must be handled accordingly.
- Reviewer preference on file (Kenny Boyd): no blame-implying rationale and no judgmental
  tier labels. Workload bands and player flags must read as descriptive, never as a verdict
  on the athlete.

## Terminology

EPA / PPA (expected points added per play), success rate, explosiveness, line yards, havoc
rate, stuff rate, snap count, exposure, workload baseline. Power Four = SEC, Big Ten, Big 12,
ACC — the comparison set for all percentiles.

## Open decisions

- Whether the two editions ship as two documents or one document with a split section.
- Whether the GPS/force-plate/VBT join enters the performance edition this season or next.

# Impeccable finish review — Baylor weekly coach report

## 1. Disposition and provenance

**Disposition: FAILS FINISH REVIEW.** 14 material findings. None is a rebuild directive — the direction is intact and every finding is patch-level (wire the unused `meta` fields, declare one play-count spine, unify one legend/polarity system, fix tokens). One fix batch is plausible.

Two disclosures, per the skill's requirement that a substituted or degraded review never be silent:

- **The named reviewer reference does not exist in this install.** `/Users/kristinarash/.claude/skills/impeccable/reference/degraded/finish-reviewer.md` is absent (there is no `degraded/` directory). I reconstructed the five-section contract from `reference/new-work.md` §105 and ran the craft floor from `reference/craft-floor.md` as given.
- **Prototype A's screenshots are stale.** `a0`–`a3` are footed "Sheet 1 of 4" … "4 of 4". The file on disk is a **five**-sheet build ("Sheet 1 of 5" … "5 of 5") and prints to exactly 5 US Letter pages. The shots show a superseded 4-sheet layout in which sheets 3 and 4 overflowed and clipped. I re-rendered both files myself with headless Chrome (`--print-to-pdf`, `@page size:letter`) and scored A against that render plus current source. **B's screenshots are current** (4 sheets, 4 pages, footers match). All sheet numbers below are the *current* ones.

## 2. Contract audit

**Prototype A — `prototype_a_analytics.tpl.html`**

| Block | Verdict |
|---|---|
| THESIS "every metric drawn against its Power Four reference range, with only out-of-range values marked" | **Partial.** Delivered fully on sheet 2 only. Sheet 1 — the sheet a coach reads first — carries no P4 reference range on any row; it compares Baylor to Baylor. And "only out-of-range values are marked" is broken by sheets 4–5, which reuse the same ▲/● marks for values comfortably inside the band (finding 5). |
| OWN-WORLD banded paper, punched rail, three inks, Archivo Narrow / Roboto Mono / Source Sans 3 | **Held in the PDF render.** Two leaks: the type is network-dependent (finding 12) and the paper/rail/bands are CSS backgrounds that vanish on a default browser print (finding 11). |
| STORY "sees two marked values in ninety seconds" | **Held on sheet 2.** The two oxide rows (Havoc created, 3rd pctl; Stuff rate, 5th pctl) read in seconds and the OUT OF RANGE prose beneath them is the best writing in either file. |
| FIRST VIEWPORT boxed header → win-prob trace → scoring events → banded rows | **Held exactly.** |
| FORM monitoring chart | **Held.** No card grid, no dashboard, no hero-metric page. |

**Prototype B — `prototype_b_demand.tpl.html`**

| Block | Verdict |
|---|---|
| THESIS "every player's snap count plotted against his own prior-week range, with only the values outside that range marked… no squad average pretending to be a baseline" | **Held in the table, broken in the narrative.** All 47 players get their own range and three rows honestly print "fewer than 3 prior games" rather than fake one — that is the thesis kept where it is hardest. But the OUT OF RANGE section narrates 4 of the 8 marked players by a hard `slice()` under a header claiming completeness (finding 7), and the out-of-range marks are clamped so exceedance magnitude is unreadable (finding 8). |
| OWN-WORLD | Same as A; same two leaks. |
| STORY "plan the training week against a projected snap demand for TCU" | **Held.** The projection is derived honestly from TCU's opponents (67 ≈ 334/5) and correctly framed as a range, not a promise. |
| FIRST VIEWPORT header → exposure observations → quarter and group load | **Held in arrangement, contradicted in content** — the exposure table is the sheet's worst data (finding 2). |
| FORM monitoring chart | **Held.** |

## 3. Material findings

**1 — Both editions hard-code the weekly variables the product exists to eliminate. `prototype_a_analytics.tpl.html` (sheets 1, 4, 5) and `prototype_b_demand.tpl.html` (sheets 1, 4).**
PRODUCT.md names one hard requirement: *"Zero weekly hand-edits. Opponent, next opponent, colors, and logos resolve from data"* — and names hand-edited opponent names as the specific failure that killed the predecessor. Both files reproduce it:

- A: `"TCU"` literal in 8 places — the sheet-4 lede, the sheet-5 heading, both column heads, and inside both narrative sentence builders (lines 290, 305, 308, 315, 317, 624, 630).
- A: `d.off === "BU" ? "Baylor" : "K-State"` (line 594) — the drive log's opponent name is a string literal.
- A: `document.getElementById("dateVal").textContent = "04 Oct 2025"` (line 380) overwrites the data-driven date; `M.next_game.replace("Week 8 · ", …)` (line 382) hard-codes the week.
- A: `"through week 6"` in the SEASON TRACE subhead (line 325).
- B: `"Wk 8 at TCU"` assigned as a literal (line 336, not even reading `meta`); `"04 Oct 2025"` (line 155); `"weeks 1 to 5"`, `"weeks 1–5"` ×2, `"weeks 1–6"`, `"week 6"` (lines 205, 218, 235, 247, 264, 291).
- B, worst of all: **line 249 is a frozen factual claim** — `"Week 6 is the widest gap of the season so far"` written into the markup, not generated.

The payload already carries `meta.next_opponent`, `meta.date`, `meta.week`. The data is present and unused. Run this unchanged in week 7 and both editions print TCU as the next opponent, 04 Oct as the date, "weeks 1–5" as the baseline window, and assert that week 6 was the worst week of a season that has moved on.

**2 — `prototype_b_demand.tpl.html`, sheet 1: the EXPOSURE OBSERVATIONS table reports two different play counts in the same rows.**
The THIS GAME column prints `box_snaps` (62 offensive, 82 defensive). The READING column prints `tempo`, which is built on 66 and 85:

- "Offensive snaps 62" beside "Plays per drive, offense **5.50**" — 62 ÷ 12 = 5.17. 5.50 is 66 ÷ 12.
- "Defensive snaps 82" beside "defense faced **7.08**" — 82 ÷ 12 = 6.83. 7.08 is 85 ÷ 12.
- "Seconds per snap, offense **20.0**" with TOP 22:02 — 1322 ÷ 62 = 21.3. 20.0 is 1322 ÷ 66.
- "defense faced **26.4**" with 37:21 — 2241 ÷ 82 = 27.3. 26.4 is 2241 ÷ 85.

Four of seven rows are internally contradictory on the sheet whose entire subject is counting exposure. This was already fixed in edition A (sheet 1 now recomputes 5.2 and 6.8 from 62/82) — the fix was applied to one edition and not the other.

**3 — `prototype_b_demand.tpl.html`, sheet 1: a third play count sits directly beneath the second.**
WHEN THE SNAPS HAPPENED, subtitled "Plays run, by quarter," sums to **85 offensive and 102 defensive** plays (21+20+20+24; 17+30+21+34) — printed two inches below a table declaring 62 and 82. Three mutually exclusive answers to "how many plays did we run" on one printed sheet, with no footnote reconciling any of them. A strength coach who adds the column will not trust the sheet again.

**4 — `prototype_a_analytics.tpl.html`, sheet 1: the win-probability chart's quarter rules are in the wrong place, and the legend asserts they are not.**
`trace()` draws three vertical rules at `mL + iw * (q/4)` — exact quarter-fractions of the **play index**. The legend reads "Vertical rules mark quarters." The payload's `winprob` points carry only `{p, wp, hs, as}`; there is no period or clock field, so quarter boundaries cannot be derived. Play distribution is nowhere near uniform (B's own quarter table: 38 / 50 / 41 / 58). Every rule is displaced, and each of the twelve numbered scoring events is therefore read against the wrong quarter. This is a fabricated axis annotation on the page whose thesis is honest chart grammar.

**5 — `prototype_a_analytics.tpl.html`: the ▲ and ● marks are redefined between sheet 2 and sheets 4–5, with no second legend.**
Sheet 2's legend defines them precisely: "● Baylor, inside range / ▲ Baylor, outside range," where *outside* means outside the Power Four 10th–90th percentile — used only on the 3rd and 5th percentile rows. Sheets 4 and 5 reuse the identical drawn marks for:
- ▲ "WHAT THEY CANNOT DO" — TCU line yards, **16th** percentile
- ▲ "WHERE WE ATTACK" — TCU stuff rate allowed, **25th** percentile
- ● "WHAT THEY LEAN ON" — TCU strength

Both ▲ values are inside the band the mark was defined to mean *outside of*. The mark now means "weakness," ● means "strength," and on "WHERE WE ATTACK" the oxide ▲ marks something **good for Baylor** — inverting the colour polarity established on sheets 1 and 2. Four meanings, two marks, one legend, and the legend is three sheets back.

**6 — `prototype_a_analytics.tpl.html`, sheet 5: SEASON TRACE puts opposite-polarity measures on one shared axis, contradicting sheet 2's stated rule, and three of six rows are unreadable.**
The legend admits it: "● Offense EPA per play, higher is better ◆ Defense EPA per play allowed, lower is better" — on a single left-to-right axis. Sheet 2 of the same document states the governing principle: *"Defensive rows are already polarity-corrected, so on every row further right is better."* Sheet 5 ships the uncorrected version.

Compounding it, the marks collide because the axis is shared and unjittered: week 1 (+0.30 / +0.29), week 2 (+0.26 / +0.26) and week 6 (+0.22 / +0.21) render as overlapping blobs. On week 2 the blue dot is completely hidden under the red diamond. In ink, half the chart's rows lose one of their two values.

**7 — `prototype_b_demand.tpl.html`, sheet 2: the OUT OF RANGE section claims to be a complete list and is hard-capped at four.**
Header: "Players outside their own prior-week range." Code: `high.slice(0, 3)` and `low.slice(0, 1)`, with the low list further filtered by `p.band.med >= 15`. The flow sheet marks **eight** players (3 above, 5 below); the narrative names four. Matthew Klopfenstein (20 snaps, median 41), Caden Knighten (11, median 21), Caden Jenkins (10, median 37.5) and Sean Thompkins Jr. (1, median 15) are marked oxide in the table on sheet 3 and explained nowhere. This week the "3 above" cap happens to be exact; on any week with a fourth, a flagged athlete is dropped silently from a section that reads as exhaustive. Sheet 4's summary compounds it — "3 players finished Saturday above their own prior range" is correct, but the sheet never mentions the five who fell below, including LaKelsey Johnson Jr. at 1 snap against a median of 26, which sheet 2's own copy calls "worth confirming against the availability list."

**8 — `prototype_b_demand.tpl.html`, sheets 2–3: out-of-range marks are clamped to the track edge, so the size of the exceedance is unreadable.**
`ownRangeTrack()` sets `lo = Math.min(b.lo, p.this_week)`, `hi = Math.max(b.hi, p.this_week)` — the axis rescales to swallow the flagged value, so every ▲ and ▼ lands at exactly the same x. Keaton Thomas (96 against a 48–95 range — **one snap** over) and Reggie Bush II (43 against a 2–39 range, from a median of 3) plot identically. The rescale also deforms the box: Bush's prior range is squeezed to make room for the value being judged against it. The one quantity an S&C coach needs from this chart — how far outside — is encoded nowhere.

Related: the marking rule itself is the least stable estimator available. Flagging Keaton Thomas for 96 against a max of 95 will read as noise the first time a coach checks it, and min/max necessarily grows more extreme every week. The payload already carries `baseline: 72.6` and `delta_pct: 32.2` for him; neither is used.

**9 — `prototype_b_demand.tpl.html`, sheet 4: the SEASON LOAD chart alarms in both directions under a lede that names only one.**
The lede: "Weeks where the defensive count runs above the offensive count are the weeks that cost the most." The chart: `const wide = Math.abs(a - b) >= 15` — absolute magnitude, no direction. So week 2 (90 off / 63 def, −27) and week 3 (87 / 58, −29) — the two **lightest** defensive weeks of the season — get the identical oxide rule as week 6 (62 / 82, +20). The GAP column beside it does handle direction correctly (`gap === maxGap ? "out" : "mid"`), so the table and the chart on the same row use opposite conventions. The dead `aBetterHigh = true` parameter in `pairTrack`'s signature is evidence the polarity question was raised and abandoned.

**10 — `prototype_b_demand.tpl.html`, sheet 4: "Week 6 is the widest gap of the season so far" is contradicted by the table under it.**
Week 3 is −29; week 6 is +20. 29 > 20. The sentence means "widest gap in the direction that costs," and says something else. (This is the same hard-coded string as finding 1 — it is both frozen and, as written, false.)

**11 — Both files: no `print-color-adjust`, on a product whose stated primary medium is print.**
Neither file sets `print-color-adjust` / `-webkit-print-color-adjust: exact`. Chrome's "Background graphics" box is off by default. Print either HTML from a browser and you lose: the alternating `#e6ece3` bands, the `.rows tr.flagged` pink ground that is the row-level out-of-range signal on B sheets 2–3 and A sheet 2, the punched-rail `radial-gradient` that is the OWN-WORLD's signature material, and the `#f4f5f1` paper itself. Meaning survives — the ▲/▼ are SVG and the oxide numerals are CSS `color`, so the redundancy holds — but the report loses its scan-ability and its world to one unchecked box. The declared pipeline (headless Chrome `--print-to-pdf`) prints backgrounds by default and is unaffected; the risk is PRODUCT.md's own scenario, "the file must survive being emailed and re-rendered."

**12 — Both files: the type voice depends on a network fetch, against a "single self-contained file" stack.**
Both load Archivo Narrow, Roboto Mono and Source Sans 3 from `fonts.googleapis.com`. PRODUCT.md's Stack: *"single self-contained file per edition… the file must survive being emailed and re-rendered without a build step."* Offline, on a locked-down staff network, or in a re-render six months from now, the OWN-WORLD collapses to its declared fallbacks — `"Arial Narrow"`, `ui-monospace`, `-apple-system`. The craft floor is explicit that this is the failure case, not the fallback case: *"the closest installed font is a failure, not a fallback."* Self-host or subset and inline.

**13 — Both files: `--ink-3` (#6d7773) fails the contrast floor while carrying every chart's denominator.**
4.23:1 on paper, **3.85:1 on the banded rows** — below the 4.5:1 body floor, at **7.5pt**. It is the colour of `.h2note`, which is where each chart's reference frame lives: "Win probability, Baylor, all 161 plays," "Values outside the Power Four 10th–90th percentile," "This game against Baylor's own season to date," "Players outside their own prior-week range." It is also the SVG axis text (`font-size: 8`) and the sources block. The smallest, least legible type on the page is the type that tells you what the numbers mean — and this is a handout that gets photocopied. Separately, `--ref` (#ccd6d9), the shaded interquartile box that is the core grammar of both editions' charts, is **1.35:1** against paper — below the 3:1 non-text floor, and it is the only encoding of "the middle half."

**14 — `prototype_a_analytics.tpl.html`, sheet 1: the READING column prints "below season" beside a positive change, and bad news is set lighter than good news.**
`readingOf()` returns `"below season"` whenever `good` is false, including the defence rows where `better: -1`. The sheet therefore prints:

- `Defense EPA per play allowed | +0.21 | +0.17 | **+0.04** | below season`
- `Defense EPA allowed, 3rd down | +0.53 | +0.48 | **+0.05** | below season`

The word contradicts the sign in the adjacent cell. Three rows above, "below season" sits beside −0.55, where it is arithmetically true — so the same phrase means two different things in one table. Use "worse than season" (or better, name the direction: "allowing more than season"). Compounding it, the CHANGE cell is muted (`class="r ${good ? "" : "mid"}"`) precisely when the news is bad: every number a coach needs to act on is the faintest number in the column, and every number he can ignore is the darkest.
